physics-e1-l1.title: Objects Attracted to Magnets and Magnetic Force · Basic Inquiry and Core Principles
physics-e1-l1.concept: Magnets attract things made of iron. Different poles (N pole and S pole) attract each other, and the same poles repel each other.
physics-e1-l1.example: A steel paper clip sticks to a magnet with a click, but a plastic ruler or an eraser does not stick.

physics-e2-l1.title: Vibration and Transmission When Sound Is Made · Basic Inquiry and Core Principles
physics-e2-l1.concept: Sound is made when an object vibrates. If you touch a sounding object, you can feel the vibration.
physics-e2-l1.example: When you hit a drum, the drumhead vibrates, and when you put your hand on your throat and make a sound, the vibration of your vocal cords reaches your fingertips.

physics-e3-l1.title: Straight-Line Travel of Light and Changes in Shadows · Basic Inquiry and Core Principles
physics-e3-l1.concept: Light travels in a straight line. When an opaque object blocks the path of light, a shadow forms behind it.
physics-e3-l1.example: If you decrease the distance between the flashlight and the object, the shadow on the screen gets bigger.

physics-e4-l1.title: The Balance Scale and the Principle of Equilibrium · Basic Inquiry and Core Principles
physics-e4-l1.concept: To balance, the products of (weight × distance from the fulcrum) must be equal on both sides.
physics-e4-l1.example: A $30\text{ g}$ weight placed $2\text{ units}$ from the fulcrum balances a $20\text{ g}$ weight placed $3\text{ units}$ from the fulcrum ($2 \times 30 = 3 \times 20$).

physics-e4-l2.concept: Builds the ability to interpret experimental data on the Balance Scale and the Principle of Equilibrium and to solve problems in real-life applications.

physics-e5-l1.title: Defining and Comparing Speed · Basic Inquiry and Core Principles
physics-e5-l1.concept: Speed is the distance traveled in a fixed amount of time (1 second, 1 minute, 1 hour). Speed = distance traveled ÷ time taken.
physics-e5-l1.example: If you run $100\text{ m}$ in $20$ seconds, your speed is $5\text{ m/s}$.

physics-e5-l2.title: Defining and Comparing Speed · Experiment Analysis and Problem Solving
physics-e5-l2.concept: Builds the ability to interpret experimental data on defining and Comparing Speed and to solve problems in real-life applications.

physics-e6-l1.title: Electric Circuit Connections and Images Formed by Convex Lenses · Basic Inquiry and Core Principles
physics-e6-l1.concept: When bulbs are connected in parallel, the other bulbs stay lit even if one bulb goes out. A convex lens gathers light to one point.
physics-e6-l1.example: Household outlets are wired in parallel so that appliances can be used independently.

physics-m1-l1.title: Equilibrium of Gravity, Friction, and Buoyancy · Basic Inquiry and Core Principles
physics-m1-l1.concept: The force with which the Earth pulls is gravity ($W=mg$), the force that hinders motion is friction, and the force with which a fluid pushes upward is buoyancy.
physics-m1-l1.example: The Earth's gravitational force acting on an object with a mass of $1\text{ kg}$ is about $9.8\text{ N}$.

physics-m1-l2.title: Equilibrium of Gravity, Friction, and Buoyancy · Experiment Analysis and Problem Solving

physics-m2-l1.title: Ohm's Law and Heat Capacity · Basic Inquiry and Core Principles
physics-m2-l1.concept: Current is proportional to voltage and inversely proportional to resistance ($V=IR$). The heat quantity $Q = c m \Delta T$ explains specific heat and temperature change.
physics-m2-l1.example: When a voltage of $20\text{ V}$ is applied to a resistance of $10\,\Omega$, a current of $2\text{ A}$ flows.

physics-m2-l2.title: Ohm's Law and Heat Capacity · Experiment Analysis and Problem Solving

physics-m3-l1.title: Work and the Interconversion of Mechanical Energy · Basic Inquiry and Core Principles
physics-m3-l1.concept: Applying a force to an object and moving it means doing work ($W=Fs$), and without air resistance, the sum of potential energy and kinetic energy is conserved.
physics-m3-l1.example: A falling roller coaster converts potential energy into kinetic energy by the amount that the potential energy decreases, so its speed increases.

physics-m3-l2.title: Work and the Interconversion of Mechanical Energy · Experiment Analysis and Problem Solving

physics-h1-l1.title: Collisions and Safety, Horizontal Projection and Gravity · Basic Inquiry and Core Principles
physics-h1-l1.concept: Impulse is $I = F\Delta t = \Delta p$. Increasing the collision time reduces the impact force. A horizontally projected object undergoes free-fall motion in the vertical direction.
physics-h1-l1.example: An airbag increases the collision time, greatly reducing the average impact force exerted on the passenger.

physics-h2-l1.title: Newton's Laws of Motion and Special Relativity · Basic Inquiry and Core Principles
physics-h2-l1.concept: Explore the law of acceleration $F=ma$, the distinction between action-reaction and balanced forces, and Einstein's special relativity (time dilation, length contraction).
physics-h2-l1.example: To a stationary observer, the clock of a spaceship traveling at nearly the speed of light runs slowly and its length contracts.

physics-h3-l1.title: The Photoelectric Effect, the Duality of Light, and the Microscopic World · Basic Inquiry and Core Principles
physics-h3-l1.concept: The photoelectric effect ($E_k = hf - W$) proves that light consists of photons (particles) that carry energy, and the de Broglie matter wave ($\lambda = h/p$) shows that matter also has wave properties.
physics-h3-l1.example: When light with a frequency greater than the threshold frequency ($f_0$) shines on a metal, electrons are ejected immediately, regardless of the light's intensity.

physics-e1-q1.prompt: Which of the following correctly describes what happens when the N pole and the S pole of magnets are brought close together face to face?

options.a: They attract each other
options.b: They repel each other
options.c: Nothing happens
options.d: The color of the magnet changes

hints: Think about what happens when different poles of magnets meet.
The N pole and the S pole like each other and attract.
physics-e1-q1.explanation: Between different poles (N pole and S pole) of magnets, an attractive force (attraction) acts, and between the same poles, a repulsive force (repulsion) acts.

physics-e1-q2.prompt: You put a steel paper clip inside a clear plastic cup and hold a magnet against the outside of the cup. What happens to the clip when you slowly raise the magnet upward?

options.a: It follows the magnet and climbs up the wall of the cup
options.b: It just stays still at the bottom
options.c: It melts away in an instant
options.d: It runs away to the opposite side to avoid the magnet

hints: A magnet's force can act through thin plastic or paper.
When the magnet moves, the clip is pulled along with it.
physics-e1-q2.explanation: A magnet's force (magnetic force) can pass through thin materials such as plastic, paper, and glass and act on objects made of iron.

physics-e1-q3.prompt: Suho carried out an inquiry in which he gathered various objects and tried sticking them to a magnet. Which of the following pairs contains only objects that stick well to a magnet?

options.a: An iron nail, a paper clip
options.b: A wooden chopstick, a plastic ruler
options.c: A rubber band, an eraser
options.d: A glass marble, a paper cup

hints: Look for things made of iron.
Wood, rubber, and plastic do not stick to a magnet.
physics-e1-q3.explanation: Iron nails and paper clips are made of iron, so they stick well to a magnet. Wood, rubber, plastic, and glass do not stick to a magnet.

physics-e1-q4.prompt: When you close a refrigerator door, it clicks shut by itself and sticks tightly with no gap. What scientific principle inside the part that helps with this is at work?

options.a: The attracting force of a magnet inside the rubber gasket
options.b: The charging energy of electricity
options.c: The sticky property of glue
options.d: The strong wind of air

hints: Something is inside the soft rubber around the edge of the refrigerator door.
It pulls the iron refrigerator body and the door together.
physics-e1-q4.explanation: The rubber gasket of a refrigerator door contains a magnetic strip, which clings tightly to the iron refrigerator body and keeps the cold air from leaking out.

physics-e1-c.prompt: [Advanced Inquiry] If you tie a string around the middle of a bar magnet, hang it from the ceiling, and leave it still, the magnet swings for a moment and then always stops pointing in a particular direction. What is the reason?

options.a: Because the Earth itself is a giant magnet
options.b: Because the wind blows only from the north
options.c: Because sunlight pulls the magnet
options.d: Because the weight of air is heavier in the south

hints: It is the same principle by which a compass always points north and south.
The Earth we live on is a big magnet with a North Pole and a South Pole.
physics-e1-c.explanation: The Earth is a giant magnet whose region near the North Pole acts as an S pole and whose region near the South Pole acts as an N pole, so the N pole of a freely moving magnet points north and its S pole points south.

physics-e1-q5.prompt: When a bar magnet is cut in the middle into two pieces, what happens to the cut ends of the magnet?

options.a: A new N pole and S pole form again on each cut piece
options.b: It splits into a magnet with only an N pole and a magnet with only an S pole
options.c: It completely loses its magnetic properties and becomes ordinary iron
options.d: Both pieces end up with only N poles

hints: No matter how small you cut a magnet, its N pole and S pole always exist as a pair.
There is no magnet with only one pole.
physics-e1-q5.explanation: In a magnet, the atomic-scale magnetic moments are aligned, so no matter how small you cut it, a new N pole and S pole always form again as a pair in each piece.

physics-e2-q1.prompt: Which of the following correctly describes what happens when you strike a tuning fork with a rubber mallet and then lightly touch it to the surface of water in a tank?

options.a: The water splashes in all directions because of the tuning fork's vibration
options.b: Ice forms in the water
options.c: The tuning fork absorbs the water
options.d: The water boils

hints: A sounding tuning fork is vibrating rapidly.
When a rapidly vibrating object touches water, the water ripples.
physics-e2-q1.explanation: A sounding tuning fork is vibrating, so the moment it touches the water, it splashes the water in all directions and creates waves.

physics-e2-q2.prompt: When two paper cups and silk thread are used to make a 'string telephone' for talking, which method lets you hear the other person's voice most clearly?

options.a: Pull the string tight while speaking
options.b: Let the string hang loose
options.c: Squeeze the middle of the string firmly with your hand
options.d: Soak the string with plenty of water

hints: Sound is transmitted through the vibration of the string.
If you hold the string with your hand or it is loose, the vibration disappears.
physics-e2-q2.explanation: In a string telephone, the vibration of the bottom of the paper cup is transmitted through the string, so the string must be taut for the vibration to be transmitted well to the other side.

physics-e2-q3.prompt: You place several grains of rice on a large drum and compare hitting the drum gently with a drumstick to hitting it hard. Which statement is correct?

options.a: The harder you hit, the higher the rice grains bounce and the louder the sound
options.b: The more gently you hit, the higher the rice grains bounce
options.c: Even if you hit hard, the height of the rice grains does not change
options.d: If you hit the drum hard, the vibration of the sound stops

hints: If you hit with great force, the drumhead vibrates more widely.
The larger the size (amplitude) of the vibration, the louder the sound.
physics-e2-q3.explanation: The harder you hit the drum, the larger the size (amplitude) of the drumhead's vibration, so the rice grains bounce higher and the sound is louder.

physics-e2-q4.prompt: You lit a candle in front of a speaker playing loud music, and the candle's flame flickered to the beat of the music. What is the reason this happened?

options.a: Because the vibration coming from the speaker made the air vibrate
options.b: Because only hot air came out of the speaker
options.c: Because light poured out of the speaker
options.d: Because the candle's wick melted away

hints: As the speaker's diaphragm vibrates back and forth, it pushes and pulls the surrounding air.
The vibration of the air reached the candle.
physics-e2-q4.explanation: As the speaker's diaphragm vibrates, it makes the air vibrate, and this vibration of the air (sound wave) is transmitted to the candle's flame and makes it flicker.

physics-e2-c.prompt: [Advanced Thinking] You put an alarm clock inside a vacuum bell jar from which all the air has been removed and set the alarm off. The clock's hammer is swinging and striking the bell, but no sound can be heard at all. What is the reason?

options.a: Because there is no air (medium) to carry the sound
options.b: Because sound turns into light in a vacuum
options.c: Because the glass wall absorbed all the sound
options.d: Because the clock's vibration became too fast

hints: For sound to reach our ears, it needs a transmitting material such as air.
A vacuum has no gas molecules at all.
physics-e2-c.explanation: Sound is transmitted through the vibration of a material (medium) such as air, so in a vacuum with no air, sound is not transmitted.

physics-e2-q5.prompt: When you play a xylophone, which of the following correctly compares the pitch of the sounds made by short keys and long keys?

options.a: The shorter the key, the faster it vibrates and the higher the sound
options.b: The longer the key, the higher the sound
options.c: The length of the key has no relationship to the pitch of the sound
options.d: No sound is made at all from a short key

hints: The shorter and thinner an object is, the faster it vibrates in one second.
The greater the frequency, the higher the pitch of the sound.
physics-e2-q5.explanation: The shorter the key, the greater the number of times it vibrates in one second (frequency), producing a higher sound; the longer the key, the smaller the frequency, producing a lower sound.

physics-e3-q1.prompt: You place three paper boards with holes side by side in front of a flashlight's beam. How should the holes be arranged so that you can see the light from the other side?

options.a: Line the three holes up on a straight line
options.b: Stagger the three holes in a zigzag pattern
options.c: The positions of the holes don't matter; place them any way
options.d: Cover the hole of the middle paper board with tape

hints: Light cannot go around a curved path.
Light has the property of traveling straight (travelling in a straight line).
physics-e3-q1.explanation: Light has the property of traveling straight (straight-line travel of light), so light can pass through all the holes only when the three holes lie on a straight line.

physics-e3-q2.prompt: You want to make the shadow of a teddy bear cast on a screen bigger than it is now. Which method is appropriate?

options.a: Move the teddy bear closer to the flashlight
options.b: Move the teddy bear closer to the screen
options.c: Pull the flashlight farther back from the teddy bear
options.d: Weaken the flashlight's light

hints: The closer an object is to where the light starts, the wider the area that blocks the light.
Try holding the object close to the flashlight.
physics-e3-q2.explanation: The closer the distance between the light source (flashlight) and the object, the larger the angle over which the object blocks the light, so the shadow formed on the screen gets bigger.

physics-e3-q3.prompt: You shone a flashlight on three objects (a clear glass plate, oiled paper, and thick black construction paper) and observed the shadows cast on the wall. Which object makes the darkest and sharpest shadow?

options.a: Thick black construction paper
options.b: Clear glass plate
options.c: Oiled paper
options.d: All three objects are the same

hints: Look for an opaque object that does not let any light through.
Most light passes through the glass plate, so it hardly makes a shadow.
physics-e3-q3.explanation: Thick black construction paper is an opaque object that hardly lets any light through, so the light is completely blocked and the darkest shadow forms.

physics-e3-q4.prompt: On a clear day, you observed the shadow of a flagpole standing in a schoolyard. The shadow was very long in the morning and evening and shortest at noon, 12 o'clock. What is the reason?

options.a: Because the altitude (height) of the Sun is highest at 12 noon
options.b: Because the speed of sunlight increases during the day
options.c: Because the flagpole gets longer in the morning
options.d: Because the wind blows the shadow and pushes it away

hints: Compare when the Sun is high directly overhead with when it shines at a slant.
The higher the Sun's altitude, the shorter the shadow.
physics-e3-q4.explanation: The higher the Sun's altitude, the more steeply light shines down from above, so the shadow gets shorter; in the morning and late afternoon the Sun's altitude is low and it shines at a slant, so the shadow gets longer.

physics-e3-c.prompt: [Advanced Inquiry] You made a 'pinhole camera' by poking a small pinhole in the front of a box and placing translucent paper on the back, and looked at a candle flame. The image of the candle formed upside down and reversed left to right. What is the fundamental reason this happens?

options.a: Because light that starts from the top and bottom of the candle travels straight as it passes through the pinhole
options.b: Because light is reflected and bent inside the pinhole
options.c: Because the air rotates the light
options.d: Because a lens absorbs the light

hints: Light coming from the top of the candle travels straight, passes through the hole, and reaches the lower part of the screen.
Try drawing the straight-line paths of the light as lines.
physics-e3-c.explanation: Light starting from the upper part of an object travels straight through the pinhole and reaches the lower part of the translucent paper, and light from the lower part reaches the upper part, so the image forms upside down.

physics-e3-q5.prompt: In a dark room, you shine a flashlight on a smooth flat mirror. What property of light occurs?

options.a: The phenomenon of 'reflection', in which light hits the mirror's surface and bounces off to the other side
options.b: The phenomenon in which light is absorbed into the mirror and disappears
options.c: The phenomenon in which light passes through the mirror and goes straight to the wall on the other side
options.d: The phenomenon in which light splits into several strands and becomes a rainbow

hints: A mirror has the property of bouncing light straight back.
The angle of incidence and the angle of reflection are equal.
physics-e3-q5.explanation: When light traveling straight meets a smooth surface such as a mirror, it changes its direction of travel and bounces back; this phenomenon is called 'reflection of light'.

physics-e4-q1.prompt: A 20 g weight is hung 4 units to the left of the fulcrum of a balance scale. What weight must be hung 2 units from the fulcrum on the right to balance it?
hints: Calculate (left distance × weight) = (right distance × weight).
The left side is 4 × 20 = 80, so on the right side 2 × (?) must equal 80.
physics-e4-q1.explanation: By the principle of equilibrium, the moment on the left ($4\text{ units} \times 20\text{ g} = 80$) and the moment on the right ($2\text{ units} \times ? = 80$) must be equal, so a $40\text{ g}$ weight must be hung.

physics-e4-q2.prompt: When an older brother weighing 40 kg and a younger sibling weighing 20 kg ride a seesaw, how should they sit to balance and have fun?

options.a: The older brother sits closer to the fulcrum than the younger sibling
options.b: The older brother sits farther from the fulcrum than the younger sibling
options.c: Both sit at the very ends of the seesaw in the same way
options.d: The older brother and the younger sibling sit overlapping right on top of the fulcrum

hints: The heavier person's side tips downward.
You must shorten the heavier side's distance so that the products of (weight × distance) balance.
physics-e4-q2.explanation: The heavier older brother ($40\text{ kg}$) must be half as far from the fulcrum as the lighter younger sibling ($20\text{ kg}$) in order to balance.

physics-e4-q3.prompt: In a balancing experiment, two 10 g weights are hung 3 units to the left of the fulcrum. How many 10 g weights are needed 1 unit to the right to balance?
hints: The total weight on the left is 20 g and the distance is 3 units (3 × 20 = 60).
Since the right distance is 1 unit, the weight must be 60 g (6 weights).
physics-e4-q3.explanation: The turning effect on the left is $3 \times 20\text{ g} = 60$. Since the right distance is $1\text{ unit}$, the required weight is $60\text{ g}$, so $6$ weights of $10\text{ g}$ are needed.

physics-e4-q4.prompt: When pulling out a nail firmly driven into a wooden board with a claw hammer, it takes much less effort to grab the end of the handle than the middle. What is the scientific reason?

options.a: Because the distance from the fulcrum (the curved head of the hammer) to the point of effort (the handle) becomes longer
options.b: Because the weight of the nail suddenly becomes lighter
options.c: Because the hammer generates electricity
options.d: Because the wooden board softly melts away

hints: Think about the principle of the lever.
The farther the distance between the fulcrum and the point where force is applied, the larger the force you can produce with a small force.
physics-e4-q4.explanation: In a lever, the longer the distance between the fulcrum and the point of effort, the larger the force that can be delivered to the point of load with a smaller force, so the nail can be pulled out easily.

physics-e4-c.prompt: [Advanced Thinking] When using a lever to lift a heavy rock, if you place the fulcrum closer to the rock (the load point), the force you press with your hand decreases. How does the distance your hand has to move down change?

options.a: The distance the hand must move becomes longer
options.b: The distance the hand must move also becomes shorter
options.c: The distance moved does not change at all
options.d: The rock lifts by itself without moving the hand

hints: When you gain in force by using a lever, you lose in distance moved.
In physics, this is called the 'principle of work'.
physics-e4-c.explanation: Using a lever can reduce the size of the force, but the distance the hand must move becomes correspondingly longer, so overall the amount of work done is conserved (the principle of work).

physics-e4-q5.prompt: Why can you move a heavy load with much less force when you load it onto a cart with wheels and push it than when you just drag it along the floor?

options.a: Because as the wheels roll, the 'rolling friction' at the contact surface becomes much smaller than sliding friction
options.b: Because the wheels reduce the mass of the load to 1/10
options.c: Because the Earth's gravity disappears over the wheels
options.d: Because the floor pushes the wheels forward

hints: Compare the size of the friction that occurs when an object slides with that when a wheel rolls.
The rolling friction of a wheel is very small.
physics-e4-q5.explanation: When wheels are used, the sliding friction between the ground and the object is replaced by much smaller rolling friction, so the friction force that hinders motion is greatly reduced.

physics-e5-q1.prompt: Which of the following is a correct scientific statement about comparing how fast objects move (speed)?

options.a: When running the same distance, the shorter the time taken, the faster the speed
options.b: When running for the same amount of time, the shorter the distance traveled, the faster the speed
options.c: Speed is the value obtained by dividing the time taken by the distance traveled
options.d: If an object is heavy, its speed is always constant

hints: In a running race, the first-place runner takes the shortest time to reach the finish line.
Speed = distance traveled ÷ time taken
physics-e5-q1.explanation: When traveling the same distance, the shorter the time taken, the faster; when traveling for the same amount of time, the longer the distance traveled, the faster the speed.

physics-e5-q2.prompt: When designing an experiment to fairly compare the speed at which a steel ball rolls down inclines with different slopes, which of the following is NOT a 'condition that must be kept the same (controlled variable)'?

options.a: The angle of the incline
options.b: The starting height (position) from which the steel ball begins to roll
options.c: The size and mass of the steel ball
options.d: The material and smoothness of the floor surface

hints: Look for the condition we deliberately change in order to investigate (the independent variable).
To see the speed depending on the slope, the slope must be different.
physics-e5-q2.explanation: Since we want to find out how speed depends on the slope of the incline, the slope of the incline is the 'manipulated variable' that must be changed, and the remaining conditions must be controlled to stay constant.

physics-e5-q3.prompt: In a 100 m race, four runners have the following records. Who is the fastest runner? (Seonu: 14 s, Minji: 16 s, Haeun: 15 s, Jiho: 18 s)

options.a: Seonu
options.b: Minji
options.c: Haeun
options.d: Jiho

hints: Find the runner who took the least time to run the same 100 m distance.
14 seconds is the shortest time.
physics-e5-q3.explanation: The distance traveled is the same $100\text{ m}$ for all, so Seonu, who took the shortest time of $14$ seconds, has the fastest average speed, about $7.14\text{ m/s}$.

physics-e5-q4.prompt: A car passed through a highway section-speed-enforcement zone (total distance 30 km) in 15 minutes. What is this car's average speed in km per hour?

options.a: 120 km/h
options.b: 60 km/h
options.c: 80 km/h
options.d: 200 km/h

hints: Convert 15 minutes into a fraction of an hour, using hours as the unit.
15 minutes = 15/60 hours = 0.25 hours (1/4 hour).
physics-e5-q4.explanation: $15$ minutes is $\frac{15}{60} = 0.25$ hours ($\frac{1}{4}$ hour). The average speed is $30\text{ km} \div 0.25\text{ h} = 120\text{ km/h}$.

physics-e5-c.prompt: [Advanced Data Interpretation] On a distance-versus-time graph, which option correctly pairs the physical quantity that the 'slope' of the graph line represents with the state of motion of an object when the slope is a constant straight line?

options.a: Speed — uniform motion with constant speed
options.b: Acceleration — at rest
options.c: Distance traveled — motion with steadily increasing speed
options.d: Time — motion in which direction changes

hints: On a graph, (change on the vertical axis ÷ change on the horizontal axis) = (distance ÷ time).
Distance ÷ time is speed.
physics-e5-c.explanation: The slope of a time-distance graph is (distance traveled ÷ time), so it represents 'speed', and a straight line with constant slope means 'uniform motion' with constant speed.

physics-e5-q5.prompt: Over the same 60 km distance, what is the difference in time taken between a car traveling at 60 km/h and a bus traveling at 30 km/h?

options.a: The bus takes 1 hour longer than the car
options.b: The car takes 2 hours longer than the bus
options.c: The two vehicles take exactly the same time
options.d: The bus takes 30 minutes longer than the car

hints: Use the formula time = distance ÷ speed.
Car: 60/60 = 1 hour, bus: 60/30 = 2 hours
physics-e5-q5.explanation: The car takes $60\text{ km} \div 60\text{ km/h} = 1$ hour, and the bus takes $60\text{ km} \div 30\text{ km/h} = 2$ hours, so the bus takes $1$ hour longer.

physics-e6-q1.prompt: You want to light a bulb by connecting 1 battery, 2 bulbs, and a switch with wires. Which is the correct condition for a 'closed circuit' in which the bulbs light up?

options.a: It must be connected without a break from the battery's (+) terminal through the switch and the bulbs to the (-) terminal
options.b: Both ends of the wire must be connected only to the battery's (+) terminal
options.c: A rubber band must be placed in the middle of the wire to collect electricity
options.d: The switch must be opened to leave a gap between the wires

hints: Current can flow only when the wire is connected without a break.
The (+) terminal and (-) terminal of the battery must be connected completely.
physics-e6-q1.explanation: For current to flow, a closed circuit must be formed that starts from one terminal of the battery, passes through the electrical components, and is connected without a break to the opposite terminal.

physics-e6-q2.prompt: Which of the following correctly compares a circuit with two identical bulbs connected in series and one with them connected in parallel?

options.a: Bulbs connected in parallel are brighter than bulbs connected in series
options.b: In a series connection, the remaining bulb stays lit even if one bulb is removed
options.c: In a parallel connection, if one bulb is removed, the remaining bulb also goes out immediately
options.d: Bulbs connected in series are twice as bright as in a parallel connection

hints: Think of how at home, even if you turn off the light in one room, the living room light stays on.
In a parallel connection, the full battery voltage is applied to each bulb.
physics-e6-q2.explanation: When bulbs are connected in parallel, the full voltage of the battery is applied to each bulb, so they are brighter, and even if one bulb burns out, the circuit of the other bulb is maintained.

physics-e6-q3.prompt: When you use a convex lens to project a very distant landscape or tree onto a screen and observe it, which describes the image formed on the screen?

options.a: An image smaller than the real object and flipped upside down and left to right
options.b: An image larger than the real object and upright
options.c: An image the same size as the real object and upright
options.d: No image forms and it just gets dark

hints: Think of the real image of an object located farther than the focal length from a convex lens.
Light passes through the lens, is refracted, and converges.
physics-e6-q3.explanation: When an object is farther than the focal length from a convex lens, a real image smaller than the object and flipped upside down and left to right (inverted) forms on the screen.

physics-e6-q4.prompt: You made an electromagnet by winding enamel wire 100 times around an iron nail and connecting a battery. What should you do to make this electromagnet pick up more paper clips (make it stronger)?

options.a: Connect more batteries in series so that a stronger current flows
options.b: Reduce the number of turns of the enamel wire to 20
options.c: Open the switch to cut off the current
options.d: Remove the iron nail and insert a wooden chopstick

hints: The strength of an electromagnet is proportional to the strength of the current and the number of turns of the coil.
The stronger the current, the stronger the magnetic field formed.
physics-e6-q4.explanation: To make an electromagnet stronger, you must increase the number of turns of the coil or add batteries in series to increase the strength of the current flowing in the circuit.

physics-e6-c.prompt: [Advanced Application] If you hold a magnifying glass (convex lens) very close to newspaper text, the letters look large and upright, but if you hold it far away, the letters look flipped upside down. Why do the letters look upright when it is held close?

options.a: Because the text is inside the lens's focal length, and an enlarged upright virtual image is seen
options.b: Because light was regularly reflected like a mirror on the lens surface
options.c: Because the retina of the eye is temporarily enlarged
options.d: Because water vapor in the air heated the magnifying lens

hints: Think about the path of light when an object is closer than the focal length.
Since the light spreads out, you have to extend lines backward behind the lens to make them meet.
physics-e6-c.explanation: When an object is inside the focal length of a convex lens, the extensions of the refracted light meet and form a virtual image that is larger than the object and upright (an enlarged upright virtual image).

physics-e6-q5.prompt: What is the scientific reason you must never touch an electric plug or an appliance's switch with wet hands?

options.a: Because ions of minerals dissolved in water let electricity pass easily, greatly increasing the risk of electric shock
options.b: Because water droplets cool the plug and make it freeze
options.c: Because magnetic force is generated in wet hands
options.d: Because electricity evaporates all the water on the hands

hints: Unlike pure water, everyday water contains dissolved electrolytes.
With wet hands, skin resistance drops sharply and current flows easily.
physics-e6-q5.explanation: When the skin gets wet, the body's electrical resistance drops sharply to a few tens of times less than usual, and even a low voltage can send a deadly current through the body, causing electric shock accidents.

physics-m1-q1.prompt: An astronaut whose mass is 60 kg on Earth lands on the surface of the Moon. Which statement about 'mass' and 'weight' on the Moon's surface is correct? (Assume the Moon's gravity is 1/6 of Earth's.)

options.a: The mass stays 60 kg, and the weight decreases to 1/6 of that on Earth
options.b: Both mass and weight decrease to 1/6
options.c: The mass decreases to 1/6 and the weight stays the same
options.d: Both mass and weight increase 6 times

hints: Mass is an intrinsic quantity of an object, so it does not change even if the place changes.
Weight is the magnitude of gravity, so on the Moon it becomes 1/6.
physics-m1-q1.explanation: Mass is the intrinsic amount of matter that makes up an object, so it is constant (60 kg) regardless of location, but weight is the magnitude of gravity, so on the Moon it decreases to 1/6 of that on Earth, about 98 N.

physics-m1-q2.prompt: You placed a wooden block on sandpaper and on a glass plate in turn, pulled it with a spring scale, and measured the maximum static friction. Which of the following is NOT a variable that should be controlled?

options.a: The roughness of the floor surface
options.b: The mass of the wooden block (normal force)
options.c: The speed at which the wooden block is pulled
options.d: The levelness of the laboratory

hints: The purpose of this experiment is to find the difference in friction depending on the 'type of contact surface (roughness)'.
Find the manipulated variable that must be different depending on the purpose.
physics-m1-q2.explanation: Since this is an experiment measuring how friction changes with the roughness of the contact surface, the 'roughness of the floor surface' must be the manipulated variable and must not be controlled to stay constant.

physics-m1-q3.prompt: When a 2 N weight was hung on a spring, its length increased by 3 cm from its original length. By how many cm does the spring stretch when a 6 N weight is hung on it? (Within the elastic limit.)

options.a: 9 cm
options.b: 6 cm
options.c: 3 cm
options.d: 12 cm

hints: According to Hooke's law, the elastic force and the stretched length are proportional to the force ($F = kx$).
The force increased 3 times (2 N → 6 N).
physics-m1-q3.explanation: By Hooke's law, within the elastic limit the stretched length is proportional to the applied force (weight). The force became 3 times as large, so the stretched length is $3\text{ cm} \times 3 = 9\text{ cm}$.

physics-m1-q4.prompt: When you lift a heavy friend in the water of a swimming pool, why do they feel much lighter than when lifted in air?

options.a: Because the water exerts an upward buoyant force equal to the weight of water displaced by the friend's volume
options.b: Because the friend's mass itself decreases in the water
options.c: Because water pressure squeezes the friend flat from all sides
options.d: Because Earth's gravity disappears in the water

hints: Think about Archimedes' principle.
An object submerged in water receives an upward force equal to the weight of the water it displaces.
physics-m1-q4.explanation: An object submerged in water receives an upward 'buoyant force' equal to the weight of the liquid it displaces, so it can be lifted by applying only a force of (weight - buoyant force).

physics-m1-c.prompt: [Advanced Calculation] A block of wood with a volume of 500 cm³ and a mass of 400 g is floated in water (density 1.0 g/cm³). When the block is at rest, what is the volume of the submerged part, in cm³?

options.a: 400 cm³
options.b: 500 cm³
options.c: 100 cm³
options.d: 250 cm³

hints: Since it floats at rest, the force equilibrium (gravity = buoyant force) holds.
The weight of the block of wood equals the weight of 400 g of water.
physics-m1-c.explanation: When the block floats on the water surface in equilibrium, the buoyant force equals the object's gravity. To support the gravity of $400\text{ g}$, the mass of displaced water must be $400\text{ g}$, so the submerged volume is $400\text{ cm}^3$.

physics-m1-q5.prompt: A steel ball weighs 10 N in air. When it is completely submerged in water, the spring scale reads 8 N. What is the magnitude of the buoyant force on the ball in water?

options.a: 2 N
options.c: 8 N

hints: Weight in water = actual weight in air - buoyant force
physics-m1-q5.explanation: The apparent weight in water is (actual weight - buoyant force), so $8\text{ N} = 10\text{ N} - \text{buoyant force} \implies \text{buoyant force} = 2\text{ N}$.

physics-m2-q1.prompt: When a voltage of 30 V is applied across a nichrome wire with a resistance of 10 Ω, what is the current flowing through the wire?

options.a: 3 A

hints: Ohm's law: I = V / R
Divide 30 V by 10 Ω.
physics-m2-q1.explanation: By Ohm's law, the current is $I = \frac{V}{R} = \frac{30\text{ V}}{10\,\Omega} = 3\text{ A}$.

physics-m2-q2.prompt: A current flows through a straight wire from bottom to top. Using Ampère's right-hand rule, in which direction does the N pole of a compass placed just north of the wire turn?

options.a: West
options.b: East
options.c: South
options.d: Upward

hints: Point your right thumb in the direction of the current (upward) and curl your other four fingers around the wire.
On the north side of the wire, your fingertips point west.
physics-m2-q2.explanation: When the right thumb points along the current (up), the circular magnetic field formed by the four curled fingers points from north to west on the north side of the wire, so the compass N pole turns toward the west.

physics-m2-q3.prompt: When water and cooking oil of the same mass are heated by a heater of the same power, why does the oil's temperature rise much faster than the water's?

options.a: Because the specific heat of the oil is smaller than that of water
options.b: Because the specific heat of the oil is much greater than that of water
options.c: Because water does not absorb heat at all
options.d: Because the oil conducts electricity

hints: Specific heat is the amount of heat needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1℃.
The smaller a substance's specific heat, the faster its temperature rises when the same heat is added.
physics-m2-q3.explanation: From $Q = cm\Delta T$, the temperature change is $\Delta T = \frac{Q}{cm}$. Water has a very large specific heat, so the temperature of the oil, which has a smaller specific heat, rises much faster.

physics-m2-q4.prompt: What is the scientific reason for leaving a small gap between rail joints when building railway tracks?

options.a: To prevent the rails from bending due to the thermal expansion of iron when temperatures rise in summer
options.b: To amplify the noise when trains pass
options.c: To help the rails stretch in winter
options.d: To reduce the weight of the rails

hints: Most solids increase in volume and length when their temperature rises.
The gap is extra room to allow for thermal expansion.
physics-m2-q4.explanation: Metals lengthen through thermal expansion as temperature rises. Without gaps at the joints, rails that expand in summer would push against each other and could cause a derailment.

physics-m2-c.prompt: [Advanced circuit analysis] Two resistors of 6 Ω and 3 Ω are connected in parallel and then connected to a 12 V power supply. What is the total current flowing through the whole circuit?

options.a: 6 A
options.b: 2 A
options.c: 4 A

hints: Equivalent resistance of a parallel connection: 1/R = 1/6 + 1/3 = 3/6 = 1/2, so R = 2 Ω.
Calculate the total current I = V / R = 12 / 2.
physics-m2-c.explanation: The equivalent resistance of the parallel connection is $\frac{1}{R_p} = \frac{1}{6} + \frac{1}{3} = \frac{1}{2} \implies R_p = 2\,\Omega$. The total current is $I = \frac{12\text{ V}}{2\,\Omega} = 6\text{ A}$.

physics-m2-q5.prompt: A thermos that keeps warm drinks hot for a long time has a 'vacuum' between its double walls and a 'silver coating' on the inner wall. Which option correctly pairs each feature with the mode of heat transfer it blocks?

options.a: Double vacuum wall: blocks conduction and convection / Silver-coated interior: blocks heat loss by radiation
options.b: Double vacuum wall: blocks radiation / Silver-coated interior: blocks conduction
options.c: Both block only convection
options.d: Both block only thermal expansion

hints: A vacuum contains no matter, so it prevents conduction and convection, which need matter.
Silver plating reflects radiant heat, which is an electromagnetic wave (infrared).
physics-m2-q5.explanation: The vacuum layer has no medium, so it completely blocks heat transfer by conduction and convection, while the shiny silver-coated wall reflects radiant heat in the form of infrared back inside, preventing heat loss.

physics-m3-q1.prompt: In physics, which situation is one in which the amount of 'scientific work' done is zero?

options.a: Carrying a heavy box in both hands while walking along a level surface at constant speed
options.b: Pushing a box on the floor 2 m with force
options.c: Lifting an object from the ground 1 m vertically upward
options.d: Applying force in the opposite direction to stop a rolling ball

hints: Scientific work is W = F × s × cos(θ).
If the direction of the force (vertically up) and the direction of motion (horizontal) form a 90° right angle, the work done is 0.
physics-m3-q1.explanation: When you walk horizontally carrying a box, the force you exert (the upward force supporting gravity) and the direction of motion (horizontal) form a right angle of $90^\circ$, so no component of the force acts along the direction of motion and the work done is $0$.

physics-m3-q2.prompt: The distance a wooden block was pushed was measured when a cart, with varying mass and speed, collided with it. Which conclusion about kinetic energy is correct?

options.a: Kinetic energy is proportional to mass and proportional to the square of speed
options.b: Kinetic energy is proportional only to speed and is independent of mass
options.c: If the speed doubles, the kinetic energy doubles
options.d: If the mass doubles, the kinetic energy becomes four times as large

hints: Kinetic energy formula: E_k = (1/2) m v²
If the speed (v) doubles, v² becomes four times as large.
physics-m3-q2.explanation: Since kinetic energy is $E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$, it is proportional to the object's mass and proportional to the square of its speed.

physics-m3-q3.prompt: A 2 kg roller coaster starts from rest at a point 20 m above the ground on a frictionless track. What is its kinetic energy at the moment it reaches the ground? (Use g = 9.8 m/s²)
hints: Conservation of mechanical energy: potential energy at the top = kinetic energy at the ground
Calculate E_p = m g h = 2 × 9.8 × 20.
physics-m3-q3.explanation: By the law of conservation of mechanical energy, all of the lost potential energy is converted into kinetic energy. $E_k = mgh = 2\text{ kg} \times 9.8\text{ m/s}^2 \times 20\text{ m} = 392\text{ J}$.

physics-m3-q4.prompt: If a car's speed on a road doubles from 50 km/h to 100 km/h, by approximately what factor does the sliding braking distance theoretically increase during hard braking?

options.a: 4 times
options.b: 2 times
options.c: 8 times
options.d: 16 times

hints: The work done by friction between the tires and the road (friction × braking distance) = the car's kinetic energy.
Since kinetic energy is proportional to the square of speed, braking distance is also proportional to the square of speed.
physics-m3-q4.explanation: The work done by friction over the braking distance $s$ absorbs the kinetic energy, so $f \cdot s = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 \implies s \propto v^2$. If the speed becomes $2$ times as large, the braking distance increases sharply to $2^2 = 4$ times as large.

physics-m3-c.prompt: [Advanced derivation] Which expression correctly gives the speed v of an object released from rest at height h and falling freely in a vacuum with no air resistance when it reaches the ground? (g is the gravitational acceleration.)

options.b: v = 2gh
options.c: v = √(gh)
options.d: v = gh / 2

hints: In mgh = (1/2) m v², cancel m from both sides.
You get v² = 2gh.
physics-m3-c.explanation: By conservation of mechanical energy, $mgh = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$ holds. Cancelling the mass $m$ from both sides and rearranging gives $v = \sqrt{2gh}$, which shows that the falling speed is independent of the object's mass.

physics-m3-q5.prompt: Why does a raindrop falling from a cloud several kilometers up not keep speeding up until it hits the ground, but instead fall at a constant speed (terminal velocity)?

options.a: Because as the raindrop falls faster, air resistance grows until it equals gravity, so the net force becomes 0
options.b: Because the raindrop loses all of its mass as it falls
options.c: Because gravity becomes 0 near the ground
options.d: Because ice falling from the sky melts and becomes lighter

hints: Air resistance grows with speed.
When gravity and air resistance balance, the net force is 0 and the drop moves at constant velocity (terminal velocity).
physics-m3-q5.explanation: As the falling speed increases, the upward air resistance grows until it balances the downward gravity. The net force becomes 0, acceleration stops, and the drop falls at a constant terminal velocity.

physics-h1-q1.prompt: Near the Earth's surface, of two steel balls A and B at the same height, A is released from rest to fall freely, and B is launched forcefully in the horizontal direction. Which statement about their motion is correct? (Ignore air resistance.)

options.a: A and B reach the ground at the same time
options.b: A reaches the ground before B
options.c: B reaches the ground before A
options.d: Depending on the launch speed, A may land first

hints: Think about the independence of motion.
Regardless of horizontal velocity, in the vertical direction the ball is subject only to the free-fall acceleration (g) due to gravity.
physics-h1-q1.explanation: Horizontal uniform motion and vertical free-fall motion are independent of each other. Both balls fall vertically with the same gravitational acceleration $g$, so they reach the ground at the same time.

physics-h1-q2.prompt: Two eggs of the same mass are dropped from the same height, one onto a cement floor and the other onto a soft cushion. Which comparison of physical quantities, from the moment each egg touches the surface until it stops, is correct?

options.a: The magnitude of the impulse is the same, but the average force on the egg on the cushion is smaller
options.b: The impulse on the egg on the cushion is smaller
options.c: The collision time of the egg dropped on the cement floor is longer
options.d: The average impact force on the two eggs is the same

hints: Since they fall from the same height, the velocity just before impact and the velocity change to rest (change in momentum = impulse) are the same.
The soft cushion deforms and lengthens the collision time (Δt).
physics-h1-q2.explanation: Because the change in momentum ($\Delta p$) of the two eggs is the same, the impulse ($I = F\Delta t$) is identical. The cushion lengthens the collision time $\Delta t$, reducing the average impact force $F = \frac{I}{\Delta t}$, so the egg does not break.

physics-h1-q3.prompt: A baseball of mass 0.5 kg is traveling at 30 m/s when it is hit by a bat and bounces back in the opposite direction at 40 m/s. What is the magnitude of the impulse the ball received?

options.a: 35 N·s
options.b: 5 N·s
options.c: 15 N·s
options.d: 20 N·s

hints: Impulse = change in momentum = m·v_final - m·v_initial
The ball bounced back in the opposite direction, so be careful with signs! (v_initial = +30, v_final = -40)
physics-h1-q3.explanation: The initial momentum is $p_1 = 0.5 \times 30 = +15\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m/s}$ and the final momentum is $p_2 = 0.5 \times (-40) = -20\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m/s}$. The magnitude of the impulse is $|\Delta p| = |-20 - 15| = 35\text{ N}\cdot\text{s}$.

physics-h1-q4.prompt: Which advanced new material, when cooled below a certain temperature (the critical temperature), has its electrical resistance drop to exactly zero and exhibits the 'Meissner effect' of expelling magnetic fields from its interior?

options.a: Superconductor
options.b: Graphene
options.c: Carbon nanotube
options.d: Semiconductor

hints: It is a representative futuristic material used in maglev trains and MRI machines.
It is a material whose electrical resistance becomes 0.
physics-h1-q4.explanation: Below the critical temperature, a superconductor shows superconductivity, in which electrical resistance becomes $0$, and the Meissner effect (perfect diamagnetism), in which it completely expels external magnetic fields.

physics-h1-c.prompt: [Advanced mechanics] An object of mass 1 kg is launched horizontally at 20 m/s from the edge of an 80 m high cliff. How far does it travel horizontally before reaching the ground? (Use g = 10 m/s² and ignore air resistance.)
hints: First find the fall time t: h = (1/2) g t² → 80 = (1/2) × 10 × t²
Then calculate the horizontal distance x = v_x × t.
physics-h1-c.explanation: The vertical fall time is $80 = \frac{1}{2} \times 10 \times t^2 \implies t^2 = 16 \implies t = 4$ s. Since horizontal motion is uniform, the horizontal distance is $x = v_x t = 20\text{ m/s} \times 4\text{ s} = 80\text{ m}$.

physics-h1-q5.prompt: What is the scientific reason that OLED (organic light-emitting diode) displays used in the latest smartphones and TVs are thinner and have better contrast than conventional LCDs?

options.a: Because they use self-emitting organic compound elements that produce light on their own without a separate backlight
options.b: Because OLED is a liquid that uses no electricity at all
options.c: Because tens of thousands of tiny fluorescent lamps are inside the OLED
options.d: Because they use steel plates instead of glass substrates

hints: LCDs require a backlight that shines light from behind.
In OLED, every single pixel is self-emissive.
physics-h1-q5.explanation: OLED uses thin films of organic semiconductor that emit light by themselves when current flows, so a thick backlight unit is unnecessary, and by turning pixels off it achieves perfect black, giving infinite contrast.

physics-h2-q1.prompt: What is the most accurate essential physical difference between an 'action-reaction pair' and 'balanced forces'?

options.a: Action and reaction act on two different objects, whereas balanced forces are two forces acting on one object
options.b: Action and reaction have different magnitudes, whereas balanced forces have equal magnitudes
options.c: Action and reaction can be combined to find a net force, but balanced forces cannot be combined
options.d: Action and reaction occur only on contact, whereas balanced forces are non-contact forces

hints: Action-reaction: the force A exerts on B and the force B exerts on A
Balanced forces: a state in which the resultant of two forces acting on one object is 0

physics-h2-q2.prompt: Object A of mass 3 kg and object B of mass 2 kg are placed in contact on a frictionless horizontal surface, and a horizontal force of 20 N is applied to push on the A side. physics-h2-q3.prompt: Which is the correct statement of the 'invariance of the speed of light' principle, one of the basic postulates of Einstein's special theory of relativity?

physics-h2-q4.prompt: Noise-canceling headphones measure external noise with a microphone, then output through the speaker a sound wave that is (   ) relative to that noise, canceling it out. Which wave property fills the blank?

physics-h2-q5.prompt: In high-speed internet fiber-optic communication, light propagates far along the fiber core without loss because of 'total internal reflection.' Which is the correct condition for total internal reflection to occur?

physics-h3-q1.prompt: Which result of Einstein's photoelectric effect experiments cannot possibly be explained by the 'wave theory of light' and is fully explained only by the 'photon (particle) theory of light'?

physics-h3-q2.prompt: A charged particle of mass m and charge q enters perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field B at speed v and undergoes uniform circular motion. Which option correctly gives the radius r and period T of its circular orbit?

physics-killer-01.prompt: A object starts from rest at point A, $50\,\mathrm{m}$ high, on a frictionless roller-coaster track. The heights of three points on the track are: point B $45\,\mathrm{m}$, point C $30\,\mathrm{m}$, point D $5\,\mathrm{m}$. Ignore air resistance and use $g=10\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$. physics-killer-01.explanation: Starting from rest, $mgh_A=\frac12mv^2+mgh$ gives $v=\sqrt{2g(h_A-h)}$. $v_B=\sqrt{2\cdot10\cdot5}=10$, $v_C=\sqrt{2\cdot10\cdot20}=20$, $v_D=\sqrt{2\cdot10\cdot45}=30\,\mathrm{m/s}$. So $v_C/v_B=2$ and $v_D=30\,\mathrm{m/s}$. Speed is proportional to $\sqrt{\Delta h}$, not to $\Delta h$ (option 1); taking D's height $5\,\mathrm{m}$ as the drop gives $10\,\mathrm{m/s}$ (option 3); dropping the factor $\frac12$ gives $\sqrt{10\cdot45}\approx21\,\mathrm{m/s}$ (option 4).

physics-killer-02.prompt: A vertical circular loop of radius $R=4\,\mathrm{m}$ is attached to the bottom (height $0$) of a frictionless track. A $2\,\mathrm{kg}$ object is released from rest on the track so that it goes around the loop. Use $g=10\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$. Which option correctly gives, in order, the minimum release height $h_{min}$ (measured from the bottom) needed to pass the top of the loop without leaving the track, and the normal force $N$ exerted by the track on the object at the top when the release height is $15\,\mathrm{m}$?

options.a: $8\,\mathrm{m}$, $50\,\mathrm{N}$
options.b: $10\,\mathrm{m}$, $70\,\mathrm{N}$
options.c: $10\,\mathrm{m}$, $90\,\mathrm{N}$
options.d: $10\,\mathrm{m}$, $50\,\mathrm{N}$

hints: At the top, $mg+N=\dfrac{mv^2}{R}$; not leaving the track requires $N\ge0$, i.e. $v_{top}\ge\sqrt{gR}$. Energy conservation: $mgh=mg(2R)+\frac12mv_{top}^2$.
With $v_{top}^2=gR=40$, $h_{min}=2R+\dfrac{v_{top}^2}{2g}=8+2=10\,\mathrm{m}$. For $h=15\,\mathrm{m}$, $v_{top}^2=2\cdot10\cdot(15-8)=140$.
physics-killer-02.explanation: Minimum condition $N=0$: $mg=mv^2/R\Rightarrow v_{top}^2=gR=40$. Energy conservation $mgh_{min}=mg(2R)+\frac12mv_{top}^2$ gives $h_{min}=2R+\dfrac{R}{2}=2.5R=10\,\mathrm{m}$. For $h=15\,\mathrm{m}$, $v_{top}^2=2g(h-2R)=2\cdot10\cdot7=140$. From $mg+N=mv^2/R$, $N=m\left(\dfrac{v^2}{R}-g\right)=2(35-10)=50\,\mathrm{N}$. Using only the height $2R=8\,\mathrm{m}$ ignores the kinetic energy (option 1); $N=mv^2/R=70\,\mathrm{N}$ ignores gravity (option 2); $90\,\mathrm{N}$ is a sign error that adds gravity (option 3).

physics-killer-03.prompt: A $2\,\mathrm{kg}$ object slides from rest from a height of $4\,\mathrm{m}$ down a frictionless curved surface, crosses a rough horizontal section of length $5\,\mathrm{m}$ (constant friction force of magnitude $11\,\mathrm{N}$ on the object), and then climbs a frictionless incline on the right. options.c: $25\,\mathrm{J}$, $1.25\,\mathrm{m}$
options.d: $55\,\mathrm{J}$, $2.5\,\mathrm{m}$

hints: The mechanical energy lost in the rough section equals the work done by friction, which equals the heat produced: $Q=W_f=fs$. The initial mechanical energy is $mgh_0$.
$mgh_0=2\cdot10\cdot4=80\,\mathrm{J}$, $Q=fs=11\cdot5=55\,\mathrm{J}$. The remaining mechanical energy is $80-55=25\,\mathrm{J}$.
physics-killer-03.explanation: Initial mechanical energy $E_0=mgh_0=2\cdot10\cdot4=80\,\mathrm{J}$. In the rough section $Q=fs=11\cdot5=55\,\mathrm{J}$ becomes heat, so $80-55=25\,\mathrm{J}$ of mechanical energy remains. The right incline is frictionless, so $25=mgh$ gives $h=\dfrac{25}{2\cdot10}=1.25\,\mathrm{m}$. Assuming the object returns to $4\,\mathrm{m}$ ignores friction (option 2); mistaking the remaining $25\,\mathrm{J}$ for the heat gives option 3; using $\frac12mgh$ instead of $mgh$ gives $2.5\,\mathrm{m}$ (option 4).

physics-killer-04.prompt: A ball is thrown horizontally from the edge of a $20\,\mathrm{m}$ high cliff and lands on the ground at a horizontal distance of $30\,\mathrm{m}$ from the cliff. hints: Horizontal: $x=v_0t$; vertical: $y=\frac12gt^2$. Find $v_0$ from the fall time; landing speed $v=\sqrt{v_0^2+(gt)^2}$, $\tan\theta=\dfrac{v_y}{v_0}$.
$t=\sqrt{2\cdot20/10}=2\,\mathrm{s}$, $v_0=30/2=15\,\mathrm{m/s}$, $v_y=gt=20\,\mathrm{m/s}$.
physics-killer-04.explanation: Vertically $20=\frac12\cdot10\cdot t^2\Rightarrow t=2\,\mathrm{s}$. Horizontally $30=v_0t\Rightarrow v_0=15\,\mathrm{m/s}$. Just before landing $v_y=gt=20\,\mathrm{m/s}$. $v=\sqrt{15^2+20^2}=25\,\mathrm{m/s}$, $\tan\theta=\dfrac{v_y}{v_0}=\dfrac{20}{15}=\dfrac43$. Adding the components as $v_0+gt=35$ gives option 1; inverting the tangent gives $\frac34$ (option 2); using only the vertical component $20\,\mathrm{m/s}$ as the speed gives option 4.

physics-killer-06.prompt: On a frictionless horizontal surface, object A of mass $2\,\mathrm{kg}$ moves at $6\,\mathrm{m/s}$ and collides with object B of mass $4\,\mathrm{kg}$ at rest; the two objects stick together and move as one. The change in B's momentum is $\Delta p_B=4\cdot2-0=8\,\mathrm{kg\cdot m/s}$, so $F_{avg}=\dfrac{8}{0.05}=160\,\mathrm{N}$. (A's momentum change $2(2-6)=-8$ has the same magnitude, consistent.) Using only $m_A$ in the denominator gives $v=3\,\mathrm{m/s}$ (option 1); using A's initial momentum $12$ in the force calculation gives $240\,\mathrm{N}$ (option 2); applying the elastic-collision $v_B=4\,\mathrm{m/s}$ gives option 3.

physics-killer-07.prompt: As observed from Earth, a star is $6$ light-years away. A spaceship leaves Earth for the star at a constant speed of $0.6c$ and arrives at the star. Time $t=\dfrac{L}{v}=\dfrac{480}{0.8\cdot3\times10^8}=2.0\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{s}=2.0\,\mu\mathrm{s}$, equal to the muon's proper lifetime. The Earth observer explains the same event by time dilation: $\Delta t=\dfrac{800}{0.8c}=3.3\,\mu\mathrm{s}=\gamma\cdot2.0\,\mu\mathrm{s}$. Multiplying by $\gamma$ gives $1333\,\mathrm{m}$ (option 1), multiplying by $v/c$ instead gives $640\,\mathrm{m}$ (option 2), and ignoring contraction gives option 4.

physics-killer-09.prompt: In the fusion reaction $\mathrm{^2H}+\mathrm{^3H}\rightarrow\mathrm{^4He}+\mathrm{n}$ the particle masses are $\mathrm{^2H}$: $2.0141\,\mathrm{u}$, $\mathrm{^3H}$: $3.0160\,\mathrm{u}$, $\mathrm{^4He}$: $4.0015\,\mathrm{u}$, neutron: $1.0086\,\mathrm{u}$. Take the energy equivalent of $1\,\mathrm{u}$ to be $930\,\mathrm{MeV}$ and ignore the kinetic energies of the particles before the reaction. Which option correctly gives, in order, the energy $E$ released in this reaction and the kinetic energy of the neutron, assuming the produced $\mathrm{^4He}$ and neutron have momenta of equal magnitude and a mass ratio of $4:1$?

options.a: $18.6\,\mathrm{MeV}$, $14.9\,\mathrm{MeV}$
options.b: $18.6\,\mathrm{MeV}$, $3.7\,\mathrm{MeV}$
options.c: $9.3\,\mathrm{MeV}$, $7.4\,\mathrm{MeV}$
options.d: $37.2\,\mathrm{MeV}$, $29.8\,\mathrm{MeV}$

hints: Mass defect $\Delta m=($total mass before$)-($total mass after$)$, released energy $E=\Delta m\,c^2$. With equal momentum magnitudes, $K=p^2/(2m)$, so kinetic energy is inversely proportional to mass.
physics-killer-09.explanation: $\Delta m=5.0301-5.0101=0.0200\,\mathrm{u}$, so $E=\Delta mc^2=0.0200\times930=18.6\,\mathrm{MeV}$. After the reaction the two particles have equal momentum magnitudes, so $K=\dfrac{p^2}{2m}\propto\dfrac1m$ and $K_{He}:K_n=1:4$. Hence $K_n=\dfrac45\times18.6=14.88\approx14.9\,\mathrm{MeV}$ and $K_{He}\approx3.7\,\mathrm{MeV}$. Inverting the mass dependence gives $3.7\,\mathrm{MeV}$ (option 2), halving the energy gives option 3, and miscalculating $\Delta m$ as $0.0400\,\mathrm{u}$ gives option 4.

physics-killer-11.prompt: Particle P enters a uniform magnetic field $B$ perpendicular to the field and moves in uniform circular motion with an orbit radius of $5\,\mathrm{cm}$ and a period of $2\,\mu\mathrm{s}$. Particle Q enters the same field perpendicular to it, with a mass $4$ times that of P, a charge of magnitude $2$ times that of P, and a speed $3$ times that of P. Ignore gravity. Which option correctly gives, in order, the orbit radius and the period of Q?

options.a: $60\,\mathrm{cm}$, $8\,\mu\mathrm{s}$
options.b: $30\,\mathrm{cm}$, $4\,\mu\mathrm{s}$
options.c: $30\,\mathrm{cm}$, $12\,\mu\mathrm{s}$
options.d: $15\,\mathrm{cm}$, $4\,\mu\mathrm{s}$

hints: From $qvB=\dfrac{mv^2}{r}$, $r=\dfrac{mv}{qB}$, and the period is $T=\dfrac{2\pi r}{v}=\dfrac{2\pi m}{qB}$ (independent of speed).
$\dfrac{r_Q}{r_P}=\dfrac{4\cdot3}{2}=6$, $\dfrac{T_Q}{T_P}=\dfrac{4}{2}=2$.
physics-killer-11.explanation: Since $r\propto\dfrac{mv}{q}$, $\dfrac{r_Q}{r_P}=\dfrac{4m\cdot3v}{2q}\cdot\dfrac{q}{mv}=6\Rightarrow r_Q=5\times6=30\,\mathrm{cm}$. $T=\dfrac{2\pi m}{qB}$ is independent of speed, so $\dfrac{T_Q}{T_P}=\dfrac{4}{2}=2\Rightarrow T_Q=4\,\mu\mathrm{s}$. Forgetting the charge ratio gives $r=60\,\mathrm{cm}$, $T=8\,\mu\mathrm{s}$ (option 1); assuming the period is proportional to speed gives $12\,\mu\mathrm{s}$ (option 3); ignoring both mass and charge ratios and using only the speed ratio gives $r=15\,\mathrm{cm}$ (option 4).

physics-killer-12.prompt: Two parallel conducting rails a distance $\ell=0.5\,\mathrm{m}$ apart lie on a horizontal surface, joined at one end through a resistor. The closed circuit formed by the rails, the conducting rod and the resistor has a total resistance of $2\,\Omega$. A uniform vertical magnetic field $B=0.5\,\mathrm{T}$ covers the whole circuit, and the rod moves along the rails at a constant speed of $4\,\mathrm{m/s}$ away from the resistor. While the rod moves $2\,\mathrm{m}$ in $0.5\,\mathrm{s}$, the magnetic flux through the circuit changes by $\Delta\Phi=B\ell\Delta x$. Which option correctly gives, in order, the magnitude of the induced current in the circuit and the magnitude of the external force needed to keep the rod at constant speed? (There is no friction.)
hints: Faraday's law $|\mathcal E|=\dfrac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}=B\ell v$, $I=\dfrac{\mathcal E}{R}$. At constant speed the external force equals the magnetic force $F=BI\ell$.
$\Delta\Phi=0.5\times0.5\times2=0.5\,\mathrm{Wb}$, $\mathcal E=\dfrac{0.5}{0.5}=1.0\,\mathrm{V}$.
physics-killer-12.explanation: $\Delta\Phi=B\ell\Delta x=0.5\cdot0.5\cdot2=0.5\,\mathrm{Wb}$, $|\mathcal E|=\dfrac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}=\dfrac{0.5}{0.5}=1.0\,\mathrm{V}$ (agrees with $B\ell v=0.5\cdot0.5\cdot4$). $I=\dfrac{\mathcal E}{R}=\dfrac{1.0}{2}=0.5\,\mathrm{A}$. The magnetic force on the rod is $F=BI\ell=0.5\cdot0.5\cdot0.5=0.125\,\mathrm{N}$ (opposing the motion, by Lenz's law), so the external force is also $0.125\,\mathrm{N}$. Check: power $Fv=0.125\cdot4=0.5\,\mathrm{W}=I^2R=0.25\cdot2$. Omitting $\ell$ gives $I=1.0\,\mathrm{A}$ (option 1); omitting $\ell$ in the force gives $0.25\,\mathrm{N}$ (option 2); multiplying $\mathcal E$ by $\frac12$ gives option 4.
